title: Optimal Ansatz-free Hamiltonian Learning In Situ
abstract: Characterizing the features of a Hamiltonian that governs a quantum system serves as a fundamental subroutine of quantum device calibration, signal sensing, and error correction. Recent works proposed protocols have achieved the optimal Heisenberg-limited scaling learning ansatz-free Hamiltonians from their real-time evolutions without fully specifying interaction structures. However, these protocols rely on both deep circuits with interleaving probes and control, and extremely short time resolution, making them difficult to implement on near- and intermediate-term in situ quantum experiments. In this work, we propose a computationally efficient, control-free, and ancilla-free algorithm that uses only Pauli product state preparation and measurement, and learns an ansatz-free Hamiltonian $H$ with $||H||\leqΛ$ in total evolution time of $Θ(\fracΛ{ε^2}\log(\fracΛε))$. The evolution time cost of our algorithm is optimal for any control-free protocols as we further prove a lower bound of $Ω(\fracΛ{ε^2}\log(\fracΛε))$. Technically, our method introduces a randomized-sampling framework that combines band-limited kernel-based time sampling with a displacement sieve for Hamiltonian structure learning. The characteristic probe time resolution depends only on $Λ$ instead of $\varepsilon$, which makes our protocol especially appealing in the high-precision regime for sensing and calibration applications. We also show that the algorithm maintains the same asymptotic total evolution time in the presence of state-preparation-and-measurement (SPAM) noise when the Hamiltonian is local after calibration. Our results demonstrate the fundamental cost of experimentally friendly Hamiltonian learning and provide a practical route to rigorous in situ characterization of near-term quantum platforms.
summary: The paper presents an optimal, control-free algorithm to reconstruct the unknown Hamiltonian of a quantum system from limited measurement data. By establishing matching upper and lower bounds, it proves that the required total experimental time scales as $O(\Lambda/\epsilon^2 \log (\Lambda/\epsilon))$. This result is crucial for advancing in situ characterization techniques on near-term quantum hardware.
main_problem: The core problem is learning an unknown, potentially complex Hamiltonian ($H$) governing a quantum system solely from time-evolution measurements accessible in near-term quantum hardware.
main_result: The authors derive the optimal scaling for total evolution time required for this task, establishing both an upper bound $O( rac{\Lambda}{\epsilon^2} \log  rac{\Lambda}{\epsilon})$ and a matching lower bound $\Omega( rac{\Lambda}{\epsilon^2} \log  rac{\Lambda}{\epsilon})$.
method: The methodology involves developing sequential measurement protocols: first, using random time sampling (displacement sieve) to identify the support of $H$, followed by cross-Pauli measurements and parity sampling to estimate the coefficients.
model_or_system: The system is an arbitrary quantum processor whose dynamics are governed by a Hamiltonian $H = \sum \lambda_u P_u$ in the Pauli basis. The focus is on implementing this learning process using only product state preparation and measurement (SPAM) access, mimicking near-term hardware constraints.
key_observables: Correlation functions derived from time evolution, specifically second derivatives of same-Pauli measurements ($C''_{P_v}(0)$) for support finding, and first derivatives of cross-Pauli measurements ($(F^{(c)}_{A,B})'(0)$) for coefficient estimation.
important_parameters: $\Lambda$ (Hamiltonian norm bound), $\epsilon$ (desired accuracy), $t_0$ (time resolution on a discrete grid).
main_assumptions: The protocol is analyzed under the assumption of local depolarization noise (SPAM errors) and relies heavily on mathematical tools like band-limited kernel sampling and summation rules for discretization.
figures_summary: Not specified, but the notes detail algorithmic steps involving sieves, random sampling, and complexity scaling comparisons.
paper_structure: The paper builds from continuous time analysis (using displacement/cross-correlation measurements) to discrete time analysis (applying summation rules), culminating in establishing optimal lower bounds for the total required measurement time $T_{tot}$.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous, resource-optimal theoretical framework for characterizing quantum hardware parameters ($H$) using only basic, noise-resilient measurements available on current NISQ devices.
